SYDNEY: Helen Haines, the Australian lawmaker who lost her legs after being repeatedly struck by a car in an attack, said on Monday (Nov 16) she had been discharged from hospital and was now focused on rehabilitation. "This is a really positive moment," Haines said in her first public statement since the Oct 19 attack, adding that she appreciated the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages she had received from people throughout Australia and around the world. "They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing." Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital after being rammed by a car outside her office in the small town of Wangaratta in the state of Victoria last month. Surgeons amputated both of her legs.

Brendan Nugent, a resident of the town of Tarrawingee within Haines' electorate, has been charged with three offences over the incident : dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official. During a court appearance in October, the accused's lawyer said his client had some mental health concerns and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. Haines, an independent lawmaker, was elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in 2022 and 2025. Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee or attending community events with relatively little security. However, concerns about politicians' safety have grown in recent years amid rising polarisation, online abuse and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterised Australian politics.

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia 's chief executive and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Sunday (Nov 15), citing people familiar with the matter. One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang's support. T he report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours. Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs , including one involving a suspected Chinese spy that raised questions over exports of the company's advanced AI chips to China.  The scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.

Intel has been sued by shareholders who accused the US chipmaker of defrauding them by concealing the impact of a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales that caused its stock price to plunge nearly 29 per cent in a single day. In a proposed class action filed on Friday (Nov 13) in the San Jose, California, federal court, shareholders led by a Michigan pension fund said Intel was too slow to disclose information about how slowing PC sales and an inventory glut would weigh on revenue. The shareholders said Intel's problems with PC sales and excess inventory outweighed data centre construction and other benefits related to the artificial intelligence boom. They also said Intel had the motive and opportunity to defraud by raising capital in mid-August, halfway through its "disastrous" third quarter, when it sold US$23 billion of stock at US$95 per share.

The sale came as Intel looked to build out its chip contract manufacturing business, a key part of Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan's business strategy. Shares of Intel closed Friday at US$59.66. Intel did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Sunday. Shares of Intel fell 28.6 per cent on Oct 30, wiping out about US$140 billion of market value, one day after the Santa Clara, California-based company projected lower-than-expected fourth-quarter revenue and profit and forecast a prolonged slowdown in PC sales. Tan told analysts that he was disappointed by manufacturing supply shortages, an "unprecedented memory crunch," and resulting softness in PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan added. Like many other large technology companies, Intel has poured money into manufacturing, but supply disruptions have made it harder to benefit from growing demand for data centre chips. Meanwhile, rising memory prices have made PCs more expensive, weighing on demand. Friday's lawsuit, led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, seeks unspecified damages for Intel shareholders between Jul 23, 2026, and Oct 29, 2026. Tan and Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner are also defendants. Intel shares are up 62 per cent this year through Friday, though they have slid from their recent peak of US$142.35 on Jun 30.

Source: Reuters/ec

The asphalt tanker vessel that struck a docked paddlewheel cruise boat in the Mississippi River at New Orleans last week experienced a steering problem in which its rudder was stuck in one position, United States transportation safety officials said on Sunday (Nov 15). The American Cruise Lines passenger vessel American Heritage, with 190 people aboard, capsized at the dock, though no one was killed in the collision. The Atlantic Asphalt tanker was headed upriver when it experienced a "steering casualty" in which its rudder stayed in a starboard position and the vessel veered toward the river's east bank, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum told a news conference in New Orleans. NTSB officials said they do not know what caused the steering problem. The tanker's voyage-data recorder was recovered on Saturday. Issues under investigation include whether the tanker's anchors were deployed and, if so, at what depth, as well as interviews with crew members and passengers, officials said. Interviews with the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt are scheduled over the next week, they said. Harbour personnel, firefighters and onlookers scrambled to pull passengers from the cruise vessel to safety after the collision. The cruise vessel toppled over into the river.

BUCHAREST: Drones have struck three commercial ships in the Black Sea near Romania's Sulina canal, Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Sunday (Nov 15), adding that his armed forces had scrambled fighter jets twice. Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said there were no casualties and that the ships' crews had managed to control the fires on board after the strikes late on Saturday. A growing series of deadly strikes on merchant ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria shows how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for the transatlantic alliance in the Black Sea. The Sulina canal is a key Romanian shipping lane which links the Danube river to the Black Sea and is used by Ukraine for exports.

Romanian officials did not identify the origin of the drones but said they were a direct consequence of Russia's war in Ukraine. "These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law," Niculescu said. "They reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine." Russia has denied targeting Ukraine's neighbours with drones. Oprea said the three struck ships were Greek-flagged oil and chemical tanker Evia Petrol V, bulk carrier Marsol and oil products tanker Ali Najafov, both under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Evia Petrol V and Marsol were struck 4 and 5 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, the defence ministry said, inside Romanian territorial waters. Oprea said a separate general cargo ship was hit by a drone late on Friday, also with no casualties. Private television station Digi24 said the vessel was Palau-flagged general cargo ship Larissa 1. "On Tuesday and Wednesday I will be in Brussels for the meeting with my fellow (defence) ministers," Oprea said. "We need the solidarity of our allies, shown through patrols with surveillance aircraft and through equipment for counter-drone warfare." France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 maritime patrols aircraft to Romania after it asked for reinforcement. Many of the ships hit in October and November were anchored near or sailing to or from the Sulina canal.

Bahrain issued two alerts of potential threats on Sunday (Nov 15), its first such warnings since September, as Iran said it had attacked a US base in the Gulf country amid uncertainty over a US-Iran deal aimed at ending the nearly nine-month-old war. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked a US military base in Bahrain in retaliation for "hostile US actions", Iran's Fars news agency reported. The Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air-defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain, Iranian state-run Press TV reported. There was no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities. Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, urged citizens and residents to remain calm and proceed to the nearest safe location, the interior ministry said. It did not provide further details on the threats.

Two days earlier the Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked a US early-warning radar in Bahrain . The US military denied this, saying it had intercepted two Iranian drones without any damage. Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have yet to produce a breakthrough, though Washington and Tehran have held off on direct attacks in the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28 and then spread across the region, with Tehran launching missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf countries. President Donald Trump has said in recent days that he might hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, but that he would maintain a US naval blockade, Reuters reported on Saturday. On another front, however, the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition fighting them have continued to exchange attacks, with the coalition saying on Sunday it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province.

JERUSALEM: The Israeli military said on Sunday (Nov 15) its forces had struck a senior militant from Hamas's military wing, which confirmed the death of one of its commanders in Gaza. Samir Abu Younis, a military leader who played a key role in planning Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel, was killed on Saturday, according to a statement from the Islamist movement's Al-Qassam Brigade. "A short while ago, the IDF and ISA struck a senior terrorist in Hamas' military wing," the Israeli military said in a joint statement with internal security agency Shin Bet, in the early hours of Sunday morning. It did not elaborate but said it would later provide further details. "He was killed yesterday evening ... in a cowardly assassination operation," the Al-Qassam Brigade posted on Telegram, adding Younis was "among the most important commanders involved in the planning and supervision of the Oct 7 attack". A security source told AFP shortly after midnight that Younis, the commander of Al-Qassam's Rafah Brigade, died in a strike "targeting him moments ago in Al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis." Gaza's civil defence spokesman, Mahmoud Bassal, told AFP the agency had received the body of Younis, 53, and said two people were wounded in the strike in Gaza's south. Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025, after two years of war triggered by the Oct 7 attack. While the US-backed ceasefire has largely subdued the fighting, Israel has kept up regular strikes in the territory. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. During the same period, the Israeli military has reported the loss of seven soldiers, as well as one civilian contractor. Israel's former army chief Gadi Eisenkot is currently locked in negotiations to form a governing coalition while his rival, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, remains responsible for military operations.
